title: Bloom filter

definition.text: A space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is a member of a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives.

facts.text: A Bloom filter is a bit array of m bits, all 0 at first, plus k hash functions; adding an element sets to 1 the k array positions its hashes select.
To test an element, check its k positions: any 0 means it is definitely not in the set, while all 1s mean it is in the set or other elements set those bits by chance, a false positive.
False positives are possible but false negatives are not, and the false positive rate climbs as items are added, until every bit is 1 and every query answers positive.
A simple filter cannot remove an element, because clearing one of its bits could erase other elements and create false negatives; the counting variant replaces each bit with a counter.

With an optimal number of hash functions, a 1% false positive rate takes only about 9.6 bits per element whatever the element size, because the filter stores no items; the data itself needs separate storage.

Bigtable, HBase, Cassandra, ScyllaDB and PostgreSQL use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for missing rows, LSM trees keep one per on-disk component, and a cache can check one so missing keys never hit the database.

Bloom's 1970 paper analyzes the trade-off between hash area size, the time to identify a message as a non-member (reject time) and an allowable error frequency, for testing messages one by one for set membership.

Its key claim is that allowing a few non-members to be falsely identified as members permits a much smaller hash area without increasing reject time, with a secondary, possibly slow test to catch those errors when necessary.

title: Counting Bloom filter
article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Counting Bloom filters

definition.text: A Bloom filter variant whose array positions are counters instead of single bits, which lets it delete elements.

facts.text: A counting filter supports delete by widening each array position from one bit to a multibit counter; a regular Bloom filter is a counting filter with one-bit buckets.
Insert increments the counters its hashes select, lookup checks that each is non-zero, and delete decrements each one.
Counters are usually 3 or 4 bits, so a counting filter uses 3 to 4 times more space than a static Bloom filter, and counters must be large enough that overflow stays rare.
The table cannot be expanded, so the maximum number of keys must be known in advance, and the false positive rate grows rapidly once the designed capacity is exceeded.

definition.text: Set-membership filters such as cuckoo, quotient and xor filters that store short fingerprints of keys and can beat the classic Bloom filter on space, speed or deletion.

facts.text: Classic Bloom filters use 1.44log2(1/ε) bits per inserted key, but any structure in the same role strictly needs only log2(1/ε), so Bloom filters use 44% more space than an optimal one.

A cuckoo filter keeps short fingerprints of keys in a cuckoo hash table; a matching fingerprint means the key is probably in the set. It supports deletions and has better locality of reference than a Bloom filter.
Compared with the Bloom filter, a quotient filter has better locality of reference and supports deletions.

An xor filter stores fingerprints in a perfect hash table and is more memory efficient (1.23log2(1/ε) bits per key) and faster than Bloom or cuckoo filters, but it is harder to create and the set cannot be modified afterwards.

title: Cache filtering with a Bloom filter
article: Bloom filter#Extensions and applications > Cache filtering

definition.text: Using a Bloom filter to remember which URLs were requested so a web cache stores an object only when it is requested a second time.

facts.text: Nearly three-quarters of the URLs accessed from a typical web cache are one-hit-wonders, requested once and never again, so storing them wastes disk resources.
A Bloom filter keeps track of all URLs users access, and a web object is cached only when it has been accessed before, that is, on its second request.
Most one-hit-wonders are never written to disk, so the disk write workload drops, cache space is saved, and cache hit rates rise.
Akamai's servers use this to keep one-hit-wonders out of their disk caches, which significantly reduces disk workload and raises disk cache hit rates.

definition.text: A geocoding method that encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

facts.text: A geohash is a hierarchical spatial index in a Base-32 alphabet: its first character identifies one of 32 cells, and that cell in turn contains 32 cells.
The world is recursively divided into smaller cells with each additional bit until the desired precision is reached, so a longer string means a more precise location and a smaller cell.
Points whose geohashes share a longer prefix are spatially closer; 9q8yy9mf and 9q8yy9vx are close because they share the prefix 9q8yy9.
Because a geohash is a plain string, a location is easy to store in a database column, and nearest neighbors can be found with simple string comparisons and efficient index searches.
Depending on its length, a geohash tells only that a user is somewhere within an area, which gives a degree of anonymity.

A geohash is a hierarchical spatial data structure that subdivides space into grid-shaped buckets, an application of the Z-order curve; removing characters from the end gradually reduces both the code size and the precision.
Data indexed by geohash keeps all points of a rectangular area in contiguous slices, which helps databases where queries on a single index are easier or faster than multiple-index queries.
The index also supports a quick-and-dirty proximity search, because the closest points are often among the closest geohashes.

definition.text: A tree data structure in which each internal node has exactly four children, used to partition two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants.

facts.text: Each internal node of a quadtree has exactly four children, and the structure partitions a two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions; each child or leaf stores spatial information.
Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees, which partition three-dimensional space.

Finding how close points are with latitude, longitude and Euclidean distance does not scale on large data sets because it is CPU-intensive, whereas a quadtree searches points within a two-dimensional range efficiently.
Subdividing a node only after a size threshold saves computation, and a mapping such as the Hilbert curve can improve range query performance further.
Quadtrees are used for spatial indexing and range queries, location-based services such as Google Maps and Uber, image processing and compression, mesh generation and sparse data storage.
A quadtree leaf cell represents a unit of interesting spatial information, and the subdivided regions may be square, rectangular or of arbitrary shape.

Quadtrees are also used for efficient two-dimensional collision detection, for solving multidimensional fields such as fluid dynamics and electromagnetism, and for image processing, where union and intersection of images are simple and fast.

definition.text: A way to find nearby businesses by building an in-memory quadtree of all locations and walking it down to the leaf that holds the search origin.

facts.text: The quadtree is an in-memory data structure, not a database; it runs on each location-based-service server and is built when the server starts.
The root node represents the whole world map and is recursively divided into 4 quadrants until no node has more than 100 businesses.

To find nearby businesses, traverse from the root to the leaf node containing the search origin; if it holds 100 businesses return it, otherwise add businesses from its neighbors until enough are returned.

Building a quadtree for 200 million businesses may take a few minutes, during which the server cannot serve traffic, so new releases roll out to a small subset of servers at a time to avoid a brownout.

definition.text: A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines.

facts.text: IDs used in social media should be roughly sorted by time, numerical values only, and highly scalable with low latency; each generator has its own pros and cons.
A UUID has 128 bits and is simple to generate without calling another service, but it is not sequential and is inefficient for database indexing, and ID conflicts, though unlikely, are possible.
A Snowflake ID is built from a timestamp, a machine ID and a serial number, with the first bit unused so IDs stay positive; it needs no network call to an ID service, so it is fast and scalable.
Snowflake implementations vary; for example, a data center ID can be added to the machine ID component to guarantee global uniqueness.
A database auto-increment column uses the database's transaction management to handle concurrent requests and guarantees uniqueness within one table.
Auto-increment IDs need network communication and may expose sensitive business data; as user IDs they give competitors a rough idea of the total number of registered users.
In the database segment approach, ID servers fetch IDs from the database in batches and cache them, each server handling a segment of IDs, which greatly saves I/O pressure on the database.
Redis can also generate unique IDs from a key-value pair, and because it stores data in memory this performs better than the database.

title: Limits of geohash proximity search
article: Geohash#Limitations when used for deciding proximity > Edge cases

definition.text: Using shared geohash prefixes to find nearby points works for most points but fails near cell borders, the poles and the 180 degree meridian.

facts.text: Geohashes that share a long prefix are close together, but the reverse is not guaranteed: two nearby points can have a short or no shared prefix.

Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian get very different geohashes, because they lie in different halves of the world.

A bounding-box search between the southwest and northeast corner geohashes retrieves every point along the z-order curve between them, which can be far too many, and it breaks down at the 180 meridians and the poles.

Distance between two geohashes reflects distance in latitude/longitude coordinates, not actual distance; despite this, geohashing has been used for proximity search in Elasticsearch, MongoDB, HBase, Redis and Accumulo.

title: HyperLogLog

definition.text: An algorithm for the count-distinct problem that approximates the number of distinct elements in a multiset using very little memory.

facts.text: Counting distinct elements exactly needs memory proportional to their number, which is impractical for very large data sets; probabilistic estimators such as HyperLogLog use far less memory but only approximate.
HyperLogLog can estimate cardinalities of more than 10^9 with a typical standard error of 2%, using 1.5 kB of memory.
It hashes each element into a uniformly distributed random number and uses the maximum number of leading zeros in the binary forms of those numbers to estimate the cardinality.
A single estimate has a large variance, so the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum leading zeros is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the estimates.

The state is an array of m registers set to 0; add hashes the element, uses its first b bits to pick a register, and keeps the larger of the register's value and the leftmost-1 position of the remaining bits.
Count combines the registers with a harmonic mean, and merge takes the maximum of each pair of registers to obtain the union of two sets.
Add takes O(1) time and count and merge cost O(m) for m registers; Redis fixes the number of registers, so its documentation treats them as O(1).

HyperLogLog is biased for small cardinalities, where Linear Counting is used; HyperLogLog++ adds a 64-bit hash, an empirical bias correction and a sparse register representation to cut memory for small cardinalities.

definition.text: Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves, and by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added.

facts.text: A region quadtree decomposes a region into four equal quadrants and so on; each node has exactly four children or none, and tree height depends on the spatial distribution of interesting areas.

A point quadtree adapts a binary tree to two-dimensional points, with four pointers per node and every subdivision centered on a point; it usually runs in O(log n) time, though k-d trees have surpassed it.
A point-region (PR) quadtree stores a list of the points in each leaf cell instead of a uniform value, and, like the point quadtree, can grow to linear height on a bad set of points.
Edge quadtrees store lines and PM quadtrees store collections of polygons, while compressed quadtrees keep only subtrees with interesting data to avoid storing many empty nodes.

definition.text: A form of unique identifier used in distributed computing that packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number.

facts.text: The Snowflake format was created by Twitter, which uses it for tweet IDs; the format has since been adopted by other companies such as Discord and Instagram.

A snowflake has 41 bits of timestamp in milliseconds since a chosen epoch, 10 bits of machine ID to prevent clashes, and 12 bits of per-machine sequence number, so several IDs can be made in one millisecond.
Only 63 bits vary, so the value is a non-negative number that fits in a 64-bit signed integer; the first bit is unused to keep IDs positive.
Snowflakes sort by creation time, and the creation time can be calculated from the ID, so objects created before or after a given date can be selected by ID.
A generator needs no network call to an ID service, so Snowflake IDs are fast and scalable.

Implementations vary: the original Twitter library splits the 10-bit machine ID into a 5-bit data center ID and a 5-bit worker ID, while Instagram uses 41 timestamp bits, 13 shard ID bits and 10 sequence bits.

title: Universally unique identifier

definition.text: A 128-bit number used to identify information in computer systems, generated without any central authority.

facts.text: A UUID is a 128-bit number, also called a GUID in software typically created by Microsoft; it is usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 hyphenated format.

UUID uniqueness depends on no central registration authority or coordination between generators, so independent parties can label information that coexists in the same databases with negligible probability of duplication.
The probability that a UUID is duplicated is not zero but close enough to zero to be negligible; for properly generated version-4 UUIDs it is one in a billion within 103 trillion of them.
Collisions in time- and MAC-based UUIDs come only from deliberate construction or error such as skewed clocks or bugs, and random UUIDs need a high-entropy source of randomness.
The meaning of the bits is set by the variant, of which variant 1 is the most common; variants 1 and 2 have versions that further define the interpretation of the UUID.

UUIDs are commonly used as unique database keys, but the random nature of versions 3, 4 and 5 and the field ordering of versions 1 and 2 can hurt database locality and performance when they are primary keys.
Reordering time-based UUIDs so the timestamp comes first averts the insertion performance loss, which is the rationale for versions 6 and 7.

notes: ByteByteGo's claim that a UUID does not guarantee global uniqueness is compatible with the Wikipedia statement that duplication is possible but negligible; stated as such, not as a conflict

definition.text: The UUID versions are the ways of filling a UUID's bits: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, or custom.

facts.text: Version 1 concatenates a 48-bit node ID, usually the MAC address of a network interface, with a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 UTC.

Versions 1, 2 and 6 rely partly on an identifier issued by a central authority and on manufacturers assigning unique MAC addresses correctly; MAC addresses can also come from sources such as virtual machines.
Versions 3 and 5 hash a namespace identifier, itself a UUID, with a name, using MD5 for version 3 and SHA-1 for version 5, so systems derive the same UUID from names without a central registry.
A version-4 UUID has six bits fixed for variant and version, leaving 122 bits for the randomly generated part, giving 5.3×10^36 possible version-4, variant-1 UUIDs.

Version 7 UUIDs are monotonically ascending, creation-time-ordered, lexically sortable keys, so new records land at the end of the key sequence, unlike random version 4, whose keys scatter across it and hurt performance.
Version 8 UUIDs are 128-bit integers with 122 opaque bits generated by any desired method, leaving one-sixteenth of the variant 1 space for private, experimental or vendor-specific identifiers.
Versions 1, 2, 6 and 7 expose the time of generation, so UUIDs can reveal when a system went live, or user growth and sales volume over time.
